n: A sudden lament: Lebanon, open your gates so fire can burn your cedars. Mighty trees often symbolize proud leaders and nations.
Wail, cypress, for the cedar has fallen! Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the dense forest is cut down. If the greatest fall, who is safe?
Hear the shepherds wailing, their glory ruined; the lions roaring, their thickets along the Jordan destroyed.

f.g: The dense thickets along the Jordan River, where lions lived (Jeremiah 49:19).

n: The Lord commands Zechariah to act out a parable: shepherd a flock doomed to slaughter. He represents God as shepherd of His people.

f.g: Sheep destined to be killed — Israel under exploitative rulers.

n: The buyers kill the sheep without guilt; the sellers say, “Praise the Lord, I’m rich!” Their own shepherds feel no pity. A picture of greedy, heartless leaders.

f.w: Blessed be the LORD; for I am rich

n: God says He will no longer spare the people of the land; He will hand them over to their neighbors and rulers.
Zechariah shepherds the flock, especially the oppressed. He takes two staffs, naming them Beauty (or Favor) and Bands (or Union).
In one month he removes three shepherds. He grew weary of them, and the flock detested him. The identity of the three is debated.

f.g: Unclear; perhaps three leaders or classes of leaders (kings, priests, prophets).

n: The shepherd gives up: “I won’t shepherd you. Let the dying die and the rest devour each other.” Rejecting the Good Shepherd leaves people to their own destruction.

f.g: I will no longer shepherd you.

n: He breaks the staff called Beauty, symbolizing the end of God’s protective covenant with the nations around Israel.

f.g: His agreement restraining the nations from harming Israel.

n: The covenant was broken that day, and the humble sheep who were watching understood this was the Lord’s word.

f.g: The afflicted sheep — the faithful few who were paying attention.

n: The shepherd asks for his wages, and they weigh out thirty pieces of silver — the price of a slave gored by an ox. An insult to the shepherd, and to God.

The Lord says, sarcastically, “Throw it to the potter — that ‘magnificent’ price they valued me at!” Zechariah throws the silver into the temple to the potter. Matthew sees this fulfilled when Judas threw his silver into the temple and it bought a potter’s field.

f.w: a goodly price that I was prised at of them
f.g: Bitter irony: “What a fine price they thought I was worth!”

n: He breaks the second staff, Bands, ending the brotherhood between Judah and Israel — the people are divided.

f.w: the brotherhood between Judah and Israel

n: Next the Lord tells Zechariah to take the gear of a foolish, worthless shepherd.

Because they rejected the good shepherd, God will allow a bad one who doesn’t care for the lost, young, injured, or weak — but devours the best of the flock. The opposite of Christ, the Good Shepherd.

f.w: neither shall seek the young one, nor heal that that is broken

n: Woe to the worthless shepherd who abandons the flock! His arm will wither and his right eye go blind — the very strength and sight he should have used to protect them.

f.g: Worthless shepherd — as empty as an idol.
